title: Which Back-Office Work Fits an AI Agent Today?
summary: Which back-office jobs an AI agent can run on its own today, which it cannot, and how operations teams pick the first one.
body_markdown:
An AI agent fits a back-office job when the job arrives often, follows rules someone could write down, and ends in a system you can check, such as an ERP, a claims register or a shared ledger. Order entry from email, quality claims intake and recurring reconciliations pass that test today. Negotiation, pricing decisions and work whose rules live only in one person’s head still need a person.


## TL;DR


- Use a four-question fit test: volume, written rules, a checkable end point, and access IT can approve.
- The jobs that pass are mostly the ones your team describes as typing: reading an email or a PDF and putting what it says into a system.
- Pick one job, run it on your real inbox, and measure the share of items the agent finishes with no human touch.
- Operations owns the agent’s work, and IT decides which connections it may use.


## What counts as back-office work an agent can do?


Back-office work is the recurring processing behind every customer-facing promise: orders keyed into the ERP, claims logged and matched to deliveries, supplier documents filed against the right purchase order, and the weekly reports built from three exports. In most large companies this work runs on email, PDFs and spreadsheets, with a person relaying information from one system to the next.


An agent takes over that relay. It reads the incoming message and attachments, looks up the records it needs in your systems, applies the rules your team already follows, and writes the result. When an item does not fit the rules, the agent routes it to a person with the reason, and keeps working through the rest of the queue.


## The four-question fit test


1. **Does it arrive often?** Dozens of items a week, at least. A job that happens monthly rarely repays the setup.
2. **Could someone write the rules down?** If a new hire could learn the job from a page of notes and a list of customer quirks, an agent can learn it too.
3. **Does it end in a system you can check?** An order in the ERP or a row in a claims register can be compared with its source email.
4. **Can IT approve the access?** The agent needs read access to where the work arrives and write access to where it lands. If IT would never grant that to a new employee, it will not grant it to an agent either.


## Which back-office jobs pass the test today?


Job Where it arrives Where it lands Watch for


Customer order entry Order inbox, PDF and spreadsheet attachments ERP sales orders Item and depot mappings per customer


Quality claims intake Claims inbox, photos, delivery notes Claims register, ERP order reference Replies and reminders that are not new claims


Recurring reconciliations System exports, bank or partner statements Exception list, ledger entries Number and date formats across countries


Document control Supplier certificates, specifications Document register with expiry dates Versions that supersede each other


Shipment exception follow-up Carrier emails, tracking updates Order status, customer notification Which exceptions need a phone call


We have the most production evidence for the first two. At a global fresh-produce company, our agents entered 1,000+ retailer orders in their first seven weeks, and a claims agent there has read more than 7,000 emails in the claims inbox and logged 1,700 quality claims from depots in 17 European countries.


## Which jobs should stay with people for now?


Negotiating a price, deciding whether to accept a late claim from a key account, or choosing which customer gets short-shipped when supply falls short all depend on context and relationships that are rarely written down. An agent can prepare the facts for those decisions, and the person accountable for each one makes it.


The same goes for work with no system of record at the end. If the output is a judgement call that nobody can compare with a source, you will have no way to measure whether the agent is right.


## How do operations teams pick the first job?


Ask the team which work they would hand over first if they could. The answer is almost always the job they describe as typing, and it usually passes all four questions. Then gather three things for the pilot: a few weeks of the real incoming emails and files, the current rules and customer lists, and the known exceptions. Real input matters because a worked spreadsheet hides the mess the agent has to handle.


A good first pilot covers one job and one inbox, and it is live on real work within weeks. The second job is faster, because the connections and master-data mappings already exist.


## Who is responsible for the agent once it runs?


The operations lead who owned the work before owns it now. That person decides the rules, handles the exceptions the agent routes, and reviews the numbers: items finished with no human touch, exceptions by reason, and corrections after the fact.


IT keeps control of access. It approves each connection once, for example the order mailbox and the right to create sales orders in named ERP companies, and the agent can act only inside those connections. Approval steps on individual outputs are available for regulated accounts that need them; most back-office agents run without one.


## FAQ


### What is an AI agent for back-office operations?


Software that does a recurring back-office job from start to finish: it reads the incoming emails and documents, looks up your business systems, applies your rules, and writes the result into the system of record. Operations teams use agents for work such as order entry, claims intake and reconciliations.


### Which back-office job should we hand to an agent first?


One that arrives often, follows written rules, and ends in a system you can check, such as entering customer orders from email into the ERP. Avoid a first job that depends on negotiation or on judgement nobody has written down.


### Do AI agents replace the operations team?


They take over the typing and the lookups. The team keeps the customer relationships, the exceptions and the decisions about rules, and spends its time on the orders and claims that need a person.


### Who owns the agent, operations or IT?


Operations owns what the agent does and how well it does it. IT owns which systems it can reach: IT approves each connection once, and the agent can only act inside those connections.
